items.title: Nutrition & deficiency diseases
items.body:
### Nutrition and deficiency diseases

**In one line**
A balanced diet mixes energy-and-growth foods (macronutrients) with tiny but vital vitamins and minerals (micronutrients); missing one causes a specific deficiency disease.

**Why it is asked**
"Match the deficiency to the nutrient" and "which vitamin causes scurvy/rickets" are among the most repeated science questions.

**The story**
Food gives two kinds of nutrients. **Macronutrients** are needed in large amounts: **carbohydrates and fats** supply energy, while **proteins** build and repair the body. Fats are the richest fuel at about **9 kilocalories per gram (kcal/g)**, more than double the roughly **4 kcal/g** from carbohydrates or proteins. **Micronutrients** — **vitamins and minerals** — are needed only in small amounts but are essential; when one is short, a named **deficiency disease** appears. For example, too little Vitamin C stops the body making collagen, so gums bleed (scurvy); too little Vitamin D weakens bones (rickets). Protein shortage has its own two faces: **kwashiorkor** (protein lacking, with swelling/oedema and a bloated belly) and **marasmus** (both energy and protein lacking, with severe wasting).

**Picture it**

| Nutrient lacking | Disease / sign |
|---|---|
| Vitamin A | Night blindness, xerophthalmia |
| Vitamin B1 (thiamine) | Beriberi |
| Vitamin B3 (niacin) | Pellagra |
| Vitamin C | Scurvy (bleeding gums) |
| Vitamin D | Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults) |
| Iodine | Goitre, cretinism |
| Iron | Anaemia |

**Terms explained**
- **Macronutrient** = nutrient needed in large amounts (carbs, fats, proteins).
- **Micronutrient** = nutrient needed in tiny amounts (vitamins, minerals).
- **kcal/g** = kilocalories of energy released per gram of food.
- **Oedema** = swelling from fluid build-up in tissues.

**Don't confuse**
- **Kwashiorkor = protein lack (oedema); marasmus = energy + protein lack (wasting).**
- **Goitre is from iodine** (a mineral), not a vitamin.

**Remember it**
"C for sCurvy, D for Dem bones (rickets), A for night-sight." Fats = 9, carbs/protein = 4.

**TL;DR**
- Macronutrients (carbs, fats, proteins) give energy and growth; micronutrients are vitamins and minerals.
- Fats yield ~9 kcal/g; carbs and proteins ~4 kcal/g.
- Scurvy = Vitamin C; rickets = Vitamin D; beriberi = B1; pellagra = B3; goitre = iodine; anaemia = iron.
- Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency; marasmus = energy + protein deficit.
keyPoints: Macronutrients = carbohydrates, proteins, fats; micronutrients = vitamins, minerals.
Fats yield ~9 kcal/g; carbohydrates and proteins ~4 kcal/g each.
Scurvy = Vitamin C; rickets = Vitamin D; beriberi = B1; pellagra = B3 (niacin).
Goitre = iodine deficiency; anaemia = iron deficiency; night blindness = Vitamin A.
Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency (oedema); marasmus = energy + protein deficit (wasting).
items.source: NCERT Science; ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition

items.title: Communicable, vector-borne & non-communicable diseases
items.body:
### Communicable, vector-borne and non-communicable diseases

**In one line**
Diseases are either "catching" (communicable, caused by germs) or lifestyle-driven (non-communicable); for the catching kind the exam wants the germ and the carrier (vector).

**Why it is asked**
Pathogen-type sorting (bacterial vs viral vs protozoan) and the disease-vector pairs are classic statement and match-the-list items.

**The story**
**Communicable diseases** spread through **pathogens** (disease-causing germs). Sort them by germ type: **bacterial** (tuberculosis, airborne; cholera, from dirty water; plague), **viral** (dengue, COVID-19, H1N1 swine flu, Nipah, Japanese encephalitis), and **protozoan** (malaria, kala-azar). Many spread through a **vector** — a living carrier, usually an insect. The high-yield pairs: malaria rides the **female Anopheles**; dengue, chikungunya and Zika ride **Aedes**; lymphatic filariasis and Japanese encephalitis ride **Culex**; and kala-azar rides the **sandfly**. The other big group is **non-communicable diseases (NCDs)** — diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer, heart disease. These are **not** passed between people; they build up from tobacco, alcohol, poor diet and inactivity, and now cause the **majority of deaths in India**, which is why the government runs population-based NCD screening (NP-NCD).

**Andhra Pradesh angle.** **Fluorosis**, caused by **excess fluoride in drinking water** (high-fluoride groundwater), is **endemic in parts of Andhra Pradesh** (e.g. Prakasam and Rayalaseema districts); it damages teeth and bones and is a **non-communicable** condition — it does not spread from person to person. **Lymphatic filariasis**, a **mosquito-borne** (Culex) disease, **has been endemic in several coastal districts** of AP and is targeted for elimination through mass drug administration.

**Picture it**

| Disease | Pathogen | Vector |
|---|---|---|
| Malaria | Plasmodium (protozoan) | Female Anopheles |
| Dengue / Chikungunya / Zika | Virus | Aedes aegypti |
| Lymphatic filariasis | Wuchereria (worm) | Culex |
| Japanese encephalitis | Virus | Culex |
| Kala-azar | Leishmania | Sandfly |

**Terms explained**
- **Pathogen** = a germ (bacterium, virus, protozoan) that causes disease.
- **Vector** = a living carrier (often a mosquito or fly) that moves a pathogen into people.
- **Reservoir** = the natural host where a germ normally lives (fruit bats for Nipah).
- **NCD** = non-communicable disease, not spread person to person.

**Don't confuse**
- **Cholera is bacterial and water-borne**, not a mosquito-borne virus.
- **Anopheles = malaria; Aedes = dengue; Culex = filariasis/JE.** Mixing these is the commonest trap.

**Remember it**
"A-A: Anopheles-mAlaria; Aedes-dengue (both A); Culex-filariasis." Fruit bats = Nipah.

**TL;DR**
- Bacterial: TB (airborne), cholera (water); viral: dengue, COVID-19, Nipah, JE; protozoan: malaria, kala-azar.
- Malaria to Anopheles; dengue to Aedes; filariasis and JE to Culex; kala-azar to sandfly.
- Nipah reservoir = fruit bats, outbreaks mainly in Kerala.
- NCDs (diabetes, hypertension, cancer, CVD) are lifestyle-linked and cause most deaths in India.
keyPoints: Bacterial: TB (airborne), cholera (water/food); Viral: dengue, COVID-19, Nipah, JE; Protozoan: malaria, kala-azar.
Malaria → Anopheles; Dengue/Chikungunya → Aedes; Filariasis & JE → Culex; Kala-azar → Sandfly.
Nipah virus reservoir = fruit bats (Pteropus); outbreaks mainly in Kerala.
NCDs (diabetes, hypertension, cancer, CVD) are non-infectious and lifestyle-linked.
NCDs cause the majority of deaths in India; NP-NCD runs population-based screening.
AP: fluorosis (excess fluoride in drinking water) endemic in parts of the state — non-communicable; lymphatic filariasis endemic in coastal districts.

items.title: Immunity, vaccines & the Universal Immunization Programme
items.body:
### Immunity, vaccines and the Universal Immunization Programme

**In one line**
Immunity is the body's defence memory; vaccines build it in advance, and India's UIP delivers those vaccines free to every child.

**Why it is asked**
Active vs passive immunity, herd immunity, the UIP launch year and disease count, and Mission Indradhanush are reliable one-markers.

**The story**
There are two ways to get immunity. **Active immunity** is made by your own body after an infection or a vaccine; it is slow to build but **long-lasting** because the body keeps **memory cells**. **Passive immunity** is borrowed — ready-made antibodies from a mother's milk or an injected antiserum; it works **immediately but fades fast**. When enough people in a population are immune, a germ cannot find new hosts and spread slows — this is **herd immunity**, which shields even the unvaccinated. **Vaccines** train the body safely by using a weakened (attenuated), killed, or part (subunit) of a germ. India's **Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), launched 1985**, is among the world's largest and now gives free protection against **12 diseases**; Hepatitis B was added in 2007 and the pneumococcal vaccine (PCV) in 2017. **Mission Indradhanush (2014)** chases down children and pregnant women who were missed, and **U-WIN** is the digital registry (built on the CoWIN model) that records every dose.

**Picture it**

| Type | Source | Speed and duration |
|---|---|---|
| Active | Own body after infection/vaccine | Slow to build, long-lasting |
| Passive | Ready-made antibodies (milk, antiserum) | Immediate, short-lived |

**Terms explained**
- **Antibody** = a protein that locks onto and neutralises a specific germ.
- **Memory cell** = an immune cell that remembers a germ for next time.
- **Attenuated** = weakened so it cannot cause disease.
- **Herd immunity** = protection of a whole group once most members are immune.

**Don't confuse**
- **Active = durable; passive = quick but temporary.**
- UIP covers **12 diseases** (not any random number) and was launched in **1985**.

**Remember it**
"Active lasts, passive is a loan." UIP = 1985, 12 diseases.

**TL;DR**
- Active immunity (self-made) is durable; passive (ready-made) is immediate but short-lived.
- Herd immunity protects the unvaccinated when most are immune.
- UIP (1985) gives free vaccines against 12 diseases; Hep-B added 2007, PCV 2017.
- Mission Indradhanush (2014) boosts coverage; U-WIN tracks every dose.
keyPoints: Active immunity = self-made antibodies (durable); passive = ready-made antibodies (immediate, short-lived).
Herd immunity protects the unvaccinated when enough people are immune.
UIP launched 1985; free vaccines against 12 diseases.
Hepatitis B added to UIP in 2007; pneumococcal (PCV) in 2017.
Mission Indradhanush (2014) raises full-immunization coverage; U-WIN digitally tracks vaccinations.

items.title: Health missions — Ayushman Bharat, ABDM & NHM
items.body:
### Health missions — Ayushman Bharat, ABDM and NHM

**In one line**
India protects health through money (insurance cover), places (wellness centres and hospitals) and people (ASHA workers), bundled under Ayushman Bharat and the National Health Mission.

**Why it is asked**
The ₹5 lakh PM-JAY figure, the 70+ Vay Vandana extension, the ABHA digital ID and the 2.5%-of-GDP policy target are frequently tested, singly and in match-the-list form.

**The story**
**Ayushman Bharat (2018)** stands on two pillars. The first, **PM-JAY**, gives **₹5 lakh per family per year** for hospital (secondary and tertiary) care to the poorest ~40% of families (chosen from SECC data) — the world's largest health assurance scheme. The second, the **Ayushman Arogya Mandir** (the renamed Health and Wellness Centres), delivers everyday primary care and NCD screening. In **2024** the **Ayushman Vay Vandana** scheme extended free ₹5 lakh cover to **all citizens aged 70 and above**, regardless of income. The **Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM, 2021)** issues a 14-digit **ABHA** health ID that links a person's digital health records. Underneath sits the **National Health Mission (NHM)** = **NRHM (2005, rural) + NUHM (2013, urban)**, whose backbone is the community-level **ASHA** worker. The **National Health Policy 2017** set a target to raise public health spending to **2.5% of GDP**. Related efforts include **Tele-MANAS (2022)** for mental health.

**Andhra Pradesh's health system (state angle)**
- **Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (Aarogyasri)** — AP's flagship state scheme. It provides **cashless secondary and tertiary hospital care** (major surgeries and treatments) to **eligible families through empanelled hospitals** (government and private hospitals that have signed up). It **descends from the earlier Rajiv Aarogyasri** community health-insurance scheme (2007, undivided AP), an early model that influenced PM-JAY. It is **among the larger health-sector allocations in the AP state budget** (about ₹4,000 crore to the Dr NTR Vaidya Seva Trust in 2026-27).
- **108** — the **emergency-response ambulance service**, which **originated in Andhra Pradesh** (pioneered via **EMRI**, Emergency Management and Research Institute, 2005) **before spreading to other states**.
- **104** — a **health information helpline** and **fixed-day mobile medical services** (a van visits each village on a fixed day) in rural areas.
- Both 108 and 104 are examples of **public-private (PPP) delivery** in emergency and primary healthcare.

**AP's health indicators** (two data sources: **SRS** — the Sample Registration System of the Registrar General — and **NFHS-5**, the National Family Health Survey 2019-21, a **survey source for state health indicators such as TFR and IMR**):

| Indicator | Andhra Pradesh | Compared with India |
|---|---|---|
| Total Fertility Rate (TFR) | About 1.5 (SRS) to 1.7 (NFHS-5) — **below the replacement level of 2.1** | India ~2.0 |
| Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) | About 24 (SRS); of the order of 30 per 1,000 live births (NFHS-5) | **Lower than the all-India average** (~28 SRS) |
| Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) | About 45 per lakh live births (SRS) | **Lower than the all-India figure** (~97) |
| Institutional births | Very high, around 96-98% (NFHS-5) | Above the national level |

**Don't confuse:** TFR = average children per woman (replacement level 2.1); IMR = infant deaths per 1,000 live births; MMR = maternal deaths per 1 lakh live births.

**Picture it**

| Component | What it provides |
|---|---|
| PM-JAY | ₹5 lakh hospitalisation cover (poorest ~40%) |
| Ayushman Arogya Mandir | Comprehensive primary care, NCD screening |
| Vay Vandana (2024) | Free ₹5 lakh cover for all aged 70+ |
| ABDM / ABHA | 14-digit digital health ID |

**Terms explained**
- **Secondary/tertiary care** = specialist hospital treatment, as opposed to basic primary care.
- **SECC** = Socio-Economic Caste Census, used to find eligible poor families.
- **ASHA** = Accredited Social Health Activist, a trained village health volunteer.
- **ABHA** = Ayushman Bharat Health Account, the citizen's digital health ID.

**Don't confuse**
- **PM-JAY = insurance cover; Arogya Mandir = the clinic.** They are the two different pillars.
- **ABDM/ABHA is digital (an ID)**, not a hospital or a cash benefit.

**Remember it**
"5 lakh for the poor, 70-plus for all, ABHA for records, ASHA on the ground."

**TL;DR**
- Ayushman Bharat (2018) = PM-JAY (₹5 lakh cover) + Ayushman Arogya Mandir (primary care).
- Vay Vandana (2024) covers all citizens aged 70+ regardless of income.
- ABDM (2021) issues the 14-digit ABHA digital health ID.
- NHM = NRHM (2005) + NUHM (2013), ASHA-led; NHP 2017 targets 2.5% of GDP.
keyPoints: Ayushman Bharat (2018) = PM-JAY (₹5 lakh cover) + Ayushman Arogya Mandir (HWCs).
Ayushman Vay Vandana (2024) covers all citizens aged 70+ irrespective of income.
ABDM (2021) issues the 14-digit ABHA digital health ID.
NHM = NRHM (2005) + NUHM (2013); ASHA workers are community health volunteers.
National Health Policy 2017 targets 2.5% of GDP on public health; AP scheme = Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (Aarogyasri).
Dr NTR Vaidya Seva: cashless secondary/tertiary care via empanelled hospitals; descends from Rajiv Aarogyasri; a large AP budget line (~₹4,000 cr, 2026-27).
108 emergency ambulance originated in AP (EMRI); 104 = health helpline + fixed-day mobile medical services; both PPP.
AP: TFR below replacement 2.1; IMR and MMR lower than all-India; institutional births ~96-98% (NFHS-5).
items.source: PIB; National Health Authority; MoHFW; National Health Policy 2017

items.title: Eradication, elimination & WHO certifications
items.body:
### Eradication, elimination and WHO certifications

**In one line**
"Eradication" wipes a disease off the whole planet (only smallpox so far); "elimination" clears it from one country or area — and India has a strong scorecard.

**Why it is asked**
The eradication-vs-elimination distinction and India's dated milestones (polio 2014, trachoma 2024) are high-frequency, and AMR is a rising theme.

**The story**
These two words are not the same. **Eradication** means a **permanent global drop to zero** — achieved for only one human disease, **smallpox** (declared eradicated in **1980**; India's last case was 1975). **Elimination** means reducing a disease to zero or below a set threshold **in a defined area**, so it can still exist elsewhere. India's elimination record is impressive: **guinea worm (2000)**, the landmark **polio-free certification (2014)**, **maternal and neonatal tetanus (2015)**, being the **first country validated for yaws (2016)**, and the WHO-validated **elimination of trachoma (2024)**. Work continues on **tuberculosis** (India targeted elimination by **2025**, ahead of the global SDG goal of 2030, through **TB Mukt Bharat** and Ni-kshay Poshan nutrition support), plus **kala-azar, measles-rubella and lymphatic filariasis**. A growing danger is **antimicrobial resistance (AMR)** — AMR occurs when **microbes evolve to resist the drugs used against them**, worsened by overusing antibiotics in people and livestock; India fights it with the **National Action Plan on AMR (2017)** and the **Red Line campaign** (marking prescription-only medicines), under a **One Health** approach.

**Picture it**

| Disease | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Smallpox | Globally eradicated 1980 |
| Guinea worm | Eliminated from India 2000 |
| Polio | India/WHO SEAR certified polio-free 2014 |
| Maternal & neonatal tetanus | Eliminated 2015 |
| Yaws | India first country validated 2016 |
| Trachoma | WHO-validated elimination 2024 |

**Terms explained**
- **Eradication** = permanent worldwide reduction to zero cases.
- **Elimination** = zero (or below-threshold) cases in a defined area.
- **AMR** = antimicrobial resistance, when germs stop responding to drugs.
- **One Health** = tackling human, animal and environmental health together.

**Don't confuse**
- **Eradication = whole world; elimination = one area.** Only smallpox is eradicated.
- Polio was **eliminated/certified in India (2014)**, not eradicated globally — wild polio still exists in a few countries.

**Remember it**
"Smallpox gone everywhere (1980); India polio-free (2014), trachoma-free (2024)."

**TL;DR**
- Eradication = global zero (smallpox 1980); elimination = area zero.
- India: guinea worm 2000, polio-free 2014, tetanus 2015, yaws 2016, trachoma 2024.
- TB elimination targeted 2025 (ahead of SDG 2030) via TB Mukt Bharat.
- AMR fought by NAP-AMR (2017) and the Red Line campaign under One Health.
keyPoints: Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated globally (1980); guinea worm eliminated from India in 2000.
India/WHO SEAR certified polio-free in 2014; maternal & neonatal tetanus eliminated 2015.
India first country validated for yaws (2016); WHO validated trachoma elimination (2024).
TB elimination target = 2025 (ahead of SDG 2030) via TB Mukt Bharat & Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana.
AMR = drug resistance from antibiotic overuse; addressed by NAP-AMR (2017) & Red Line campaign.

items.title: Nutrition programmes & recent outbreaks
items.body:
### Nutrition programmes and recent outbreaks

**In one line**
A cluster of schemes attacks malnutrition from birth to school age, while a set of recent outbreaks (Nipah, Mpox, HMPV) keeps outbreak-preparedness and One Health in the news.

**Why it is asked**
Scheme-to-focus matching and current-affairs outbreak facts (Mpox PHEIC 2024, HMPV 2025) are directly examinable.

**The story**
India tackles malnutrition across the life cycle. **POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018)** is the overarching mission against stunting, wasting, anaemia and low birth weight, now folded into **Mission POSHAN 2.0 / Saksham Anganwadi**. **PM POSHAN (2021)** is the renamed **Mid-Day Meal Scheme**, giving hot cooked meals to school children. **Anaemia Mukt Bharat** uses a "6x6x6" strategy (six groups, six interventions, six institutions). The oldest pillar, **ICDS (1975)**, runs **Anganwadi** services for children under six and for pregnant and nursing mothers. On the disease front, recent alerts shape policy: **Nipah** recurs in **Kerala** from a fruit-bat reservoir with high case-fatality, contained by containment zones and contact tracing; the WHO declared **Mpox (monkeypox) a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in August 2024**; **HMPV (human metapneumovirus)**, a respiratory virus, drew attention in **early 2025**; and COVID-19 reinforced pandemic preparedness and the **One Health** approach. Key institutions are **ICMR** (biomedical research), **CDSCO** (the central drug regulator) and the **AIIMS** network.

**Picture it**

| Programme | Focus |
|---|---|
| POSHAN Abhiyaan / POSHAN 2.0 | Overall malnutrition and stunting |
| PM POSHAN (2021) | Hot cooked mid-day meals in schools |
| Anaemia Mukt Bharat | Reducing anaemia across age groups |
| ICDS (1975) | Anganwadi services for under-6s and mothers |

**Terms explained**
- **Stunting** = low height-for-age from chronic undernutrition.
- **Wasting** = low weight-for-height from acute undernutrition.
- **PHEIC** = Public Health Emergency of International Concern, the WHO's highest alarm.
- **Zoonosis** = a disease that jumps from animals to humans (Nipah, Mpox).

**Don't confuse**
- **PM POSHAN is the mid-day meal; POSHAN Abhiyaan is the broader mission.** They are not the same scheme.
- **Mpox PHEIC was 2024; HMPV attention was 2025** — keep the years apart.

**Remember it**
"POSHAN = nutrition mission; PM POSHAN = plate of food." Mpox 2024, HMPV 2025.

**TL;DR**
- POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) fights malnutrition; PM POSHAN (2021) = renamed mid-day meal.
- Anaemia Mukt Bharat uses a 6x6x6 strategy; ICDS (1975) runs Anganwadis.
- Nipah recurs in Kerala (fruit-bat reservoir, high fatality).
- Mpox PHEIC August 2024; HMPV early 2025; One Health links human-animal-environment.
keyPoints: POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018) fights malnutrition/stunting; PM POSHAN (2021) = renamed Mid-Day Meal.
Anaemia Mukt Bharat uses a 6x6x6 strategy; ICDS (1975) delivers Anganwadi services.
Nipah (fruit-bat reservoir) recurs in Kerala with high case-fatality.
WHO declared Mpox a PHEIC in August 2024; HMPV drew attention in early 2025.
ICMR = biomedical research; CDSCO = central drug regulator; One Health links human-animal-environment.
items.source: Ministry of Women & Child Development; WHO; MoHFW; PIB

items.title: Immunity, Vaccine Platforms & Microbiology Concepts
items.body:
### Immune cells, vaccine platforms and microbiology

**In one line**
This note nails the fine distinctions APPSC tests: which immune cell does what, which vaccine uses which technology, and the quirks of viruses, biofilms and probiotics.

**Why it is asked**
Statement-based items turn on exact facts — Covishield is a vector not an mRNA vaccine, adenovirus is DNA, probiotics do occur in the gut.

**The story**
**B cells and T cells** are lymphocytes (white blood cells) whose job is to **protect the body from diseases caused by pathogens** — they are not about allergens, body temperature or water balance. The adaptive immune system has two arms. **B cells** make **antibodies** (this is **humoral immunity**), while **T cells** run **cell-mediated immunity** — helper T cells coordinate the response and cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. Vaccines deliver their training in different ways, called **platforms**: **Covishield** is a **viral-vector** vaccine (ChAdOx1), **not** mRNA; **Covaxin** is an **inactivated** whole virus; **Sputnik V** is a viral vector; **Pfizer/Moderna** are **mRNA**; and **ZyCoV-D** is a **DNA** vaccine (the world's first). Viruses are more versatile than people think: they can infect **bacteria (as bacteriophages), fungi (mycoviruses) and plants**, not only animals. An **adenovirus** is a **double-stranded DNA** virus (a common-cold cause), whereas a **retrovirus** carries **RNA** and reverse-transcribes it into DNA — **HIV**, which causes AIDS, is a retrovirus. The receptor **ACE2** is the doorway **SARS-CoV-2** uses to enter human cells. Finally, **biofilms** — slimy microbial communities on medical implants and food surfaces — are highly **antibiotic-resistant** — they **can exhibit greater resistance to antibiotics** (10 to 1000 times) than free-floating microbes, while **probiotics** contain both **bacteria and yeast**, **do naturally occur in the gut**, and help digest **milk sugar (lactose)**.

**Picture it**

| Vaccine | Platform |
|---|---|
| Covishield | Viral vector (ChAdOx1) — not mRNA |
| Covaxin | Inactivated whole virus |
| Sputnik V | Viral vector (adenovirus) |
| Pfizer / Moderna | mRNA |
| ZyCoV-D | DNA (world's first) |

**Terms explained**
- **Humoral immunity** = defence by antibodies in body fluids (B cells).
- **Cell-mediated immunity** = defence by T cells attacking infected cells.
- **Retrovirus** = an RNA virus that copies its RNA into DNA using reverse transcriptase.
- **Biofilm** = a community of microbes stuck to a surface, protected from drugs.

**Don't confuse**
- **Covishield is a viral vector, NOT mRNA** — the single most common trap here.
- **Adenovirus = DNA; retrovirus (HIV) = RNA.**
- **Probiotics DO occur naturally in the gut** — the statement saying they do not is false.

**Remember it**
"B for aBodies, T for aTack." Covishield = vector; ZyCoV-D = DNA first.

**TL;DR**
- B cells = antibodies (humoral); T cells = cell-mediated immunity.
- Covishield = viral vector (not mRNA); Covaxin = inactivated; ZyCoV-D = world's first DNA vaccine.
- Viruses infect bacteria (phages), fungi and plants; adenovirus = DNA, retrovirus (HIV) = RNA.
- ACE2 = SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor; biofilms resist antibiotics; probiotics occur in the gut.
keyPoints: B cells make antibodies (humoral immunity); T cells provide cell-mediated immunity.
Covishield = viral vector (not mRNA); Covaxin = inactivated; Sputnik V = viral vector; ZyCoV-D = world's first DNA vaccine.
Viruses can infect bacteria (bacteriophages), fungi and plants, not only animals.
Adenovirus is a DNA virus; a retrovirus (RNA) like HIV reverse-transcribes to DNA.
ACE2 is the receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter human cells.
Biofilms form on implants and food surfaces and are highly antibiotic-resistant.
Probiotics contain bacteria and yeast, naturally occur in the gut and help digest lactose.
Ebola's 2014 outbreak centred on Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia.
items.source: ICMR/WHO fact sheets; NIV Pune; UPSC-standard S&T references (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Disease Directory I — Bacterial, Fungal & Worm Diseases
items.body:
## Which germ, which disease, how it spreads

**In one line:** bacteria cause TB, leprosy, cholera, typhoid, diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, plague, leptospirosis and scrub typhus; fungi cause ringworm and mucormycosis; worms cause filariasis, roundworm and guinea-worm disease — and antibiotics work only against bacteria.

**Why it is asked:** "Widal test is for", "leprosy is caused by", "rat-urine disease after floods", "black fungus in COVID patients", "Robert Koch discovered" and "which disease is caused by a worm" are classic match items in APPSC, UPSC and SSC papers.

**The story**

**Bacteria** are single-celled living organisms, so **antibiotics** can kill them — but antibiotics do nothing against viruses. **Robert Koch** found the TB germ, **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**, on **24 March 1882** — now World TB Day; the **BCG** vaccine protects children against severe TB. Its cousin **Mycobacterium leprae** causes leprosy (Hansen's disease); India declared leprosy **eliminated as a public-health problem in 2005** (fewer than 1 case per 10,000 people). **Cholera** (Vibrio cholerae) and **typhoid** (Salmonella typhi, diagnosed by the **Widal test**) spread through dirty water and food. **Tetanus** (Clostridium tetani) enters through wounds; **diphtheria**, **whooping cough (pertussis)** and **pneumonia** spread through the air. **Plague** (Yersinia pestis) is carried by the **rat flea**, **leptospirosis** spreads through **rat urine in flood water**, and **scrub typhus** is passed by **mite (chigger) bites**.

**Fungi** cause **ringworm** and **athlete's foot** (skin), **candidiasis** and **mucormycosis ("black fungus")**, which struck many COVID-19 patients in 2021. **Worms (helminths)** cause **ascariasis (roundworm)**, **hookworm** anaemia, **tapeworm** infection from undercooked pork, **filariasis** (Wuchereria bancrofti, spread by Culex) and **guinea-worm disease** (Dracunculus, from contaminated drinking water).

### Bacterial diseases

| Disease | Pathogen and spread |
|---|---|
| **Tuberculosis** | Mycobacterium tuberculosis — airborne; discovered by Robert Koch (1882); BCG vaccine |
| **Leprosy (Hansen's disease)** | Mycobacterium leprae — long close contact; eliminated as a public-health problem in India in 2005 |
| **Cholera** | Vibrio cholerae — contaminated water; severe watery diarrhoea |
| **Typhoid** | Salmonella typhi — food and water; Widal test |
| **Diphtheria** | Corynebacterium diphtheriae — airborne; affects the throat |
| **Tetanus** | Clostridium tetani — enters through wounds; causes lockjaw |
| **Whooping cough (pertussis)** | Bordetella pertussis — airborne |
| **Plague** | Yersinia pestis — spread by the rat flea |
| **Leptospirosis** | Leptospira — rat urine in flood water ("rat fever") |
| **Scrub typhus** | Orientia tsutsugamushi — bite of infected mites (chiggers) |
| **Anthrax** | Bacillus anthracis — from infected animals and spores |
| **Pneumonia** | often Streptococcus pneumoniae — airborne; prevented by PCV |
| **Syphilis** | Treponema pallidum — sexually transmitted |
| **Botulism** | Clostridium botulinum toxin — badly canned food |

### Fungal and worm (helminth) diseases

| Disease | Cause and spread |
|---|---|
| **Ringworm** | a fungal skin infection — not a worm |
| **Athlete's foot** | fungal infection between the toes |
| **Candidiasis** | yeast (Candida) infection of mouth, skin or genitals |
| **Mucormycosis ("black fungus")** | fungal infection seen in many COVID-19 patients in 2021, especially diabetics given steroids |
| **Ascariasis** | roundworm Ascaris — eggs in contaminated soil and food |
| **Hookworm disease** | larvae enter through bare feet; cause anaemia |
| **Taeniasis** | tapeworm Taenia — undercooked pork or beef |
| **Filariasis (elephantiasis)** | Wuchereria bancrofti worm — spread by Culex mosquito |
| **Guinea-worm disease (dracunculiasis)** | Dracunculus medinensis — drinking water with infected water fleas |
| **National Deworming Day** | held in February and August — albendazole tablets for children aged 1–19 |

## Don't confuse
- **Ringworm is a fungus, not a worm.** **Guinea worm and filaria are real worms.**
- **Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses** — they do not cure flu or COVID-19.
- **Leprosy and TB** are both Mycobacterium; **tetanus and botulism** are both Clostridium.
- **Plague = rat flea; leptospirosis = rat urine; scrub typhus = mite.**

**Remember it:** "Widal for typhoid, Koch for TB, flea for plague."

**TL;DR**
- TB (Koch 1882, BCG), leprosy (eliminated 2005), cholera (water), typhoid (Widal), tetanus (wounds), plague (rat flea), leptospirosis (rat urine), scrub typhus (mites).
- Fungal: ringworm, athlete's foot, candidiasis, mucormycosis (2021).
- Worms: Ascaris, hookworm, tapeworm, filaria (Culex), guinea worm; deworming with albendazole.
keyPoints: Tuberculosis — Mycobacterium tuberculosis — airborne; discovered by Robert Koch (1882); BCG vaccine.
Leprosy (Hansen's disease) — Mycobacterium leprae — long close contact; eliminated as a public-health problem in India in 2005.
Ringworm — a fungal skin infection — not a worm.
Mucormycosis ("black fungus") — fungal infection seen in many COVID-19 patients in 2021, especially diabetics given steroids.

items.title: Disease Directory II — Viral, Protozoan & Prion Diseases
items.body:
## Viruses, protozoa and prions

**In one line:** viruses cause polio, measles, chickenpox, rabies, hepatitis, influenza, HIV/AIDS, dengue, chikungunya, Zika, Japanese encephalitis, Kyasanur Forest Disease, Nipah, Ebola and mpox; protozoa cause malaria, kala-azar, amoebic dysentery and sleeping sickness; prions cause mad cow disease.

**Why it is asked:** "which hepatitis spreads through blood", "monkey fever (KFD) is in which state", "Chandipura virus is spread by", "the most dangerous malaria parasite", "Ronald Ross proved", "diseases spread by tattooing" (UPSC 2013) and "Zika spreads by Aedes and sexually" (UPSC 2017) are favourite items.

**The story**

Viruses are not cells: they multiply only inside a host. **Hepatitis A and E** spread through **contaminated food and water**; **hepatitis B and C** through **blood, needles and sex** — so **hepatitis B and HIV**, but **not chikungunya**, can spread through unclean tattooing needles. **HIV**, a retrovirus, destroys **CD4 helper T cells** and is screened by **ELISA**. **Rabies** comes from the bite of an infected dog; **Louis Pasteur** made the first rabies vaccine (1885). **Kyasanur Forest Disease ("monkey fever")** is a tick-borne virus first found in **Karnataka (1957)**; **Chandipura virus** is spread by **sandflies** and caused deaths among children in **Gujarat in 2024**. **Zika** spreads through **Aedes** mosquitoes and also **sexually**.

Among protozoa, **Plasmodium falciparum** causes the most dangerous (cerebral) malaria and **P. vivax** is the commonest in India. **Ronald Ross** proved mosquitoes carry malaria while working at **Secunderabad (1897)** and won the **1902 Nobel Prize**. **Kala-azar** (Leishmania donovani, sandfly) is concentrated in **Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh**. **Prions** — misfolded proteins, not living germs — cause **mad cow disease (BSE)** and **Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease** in humans.

### Viral diseases

| Disease | Virus and spread |
|---|---|
| **Polio** | poliovirus — faecal-oral; Salk (injectable, killed) and Sabin (oral, live) vaccines |
| **Measles** | airborne virus — prevented by the MR (measles-rubella) vaccine |
| **Chickenpox** | varicella-zoster virus — airborne; later reactivation causes shingles |
| **Rabies** | lyssavirus — bite of an infected dog; nearly always fatal once symptoms appear; Pasteur vaccine (1885) |
| **Hepatitis A and E** | faecal-oral — contaminated food and water |
| **Hepatitis B and C** | blood, needles and sex; B has a vaccine (in UIP) |
| **Spread by unclean tattooing needles (UPSC 2013)** | hepatitis B and HIV — not chikungunya (which needs a mosquito) |
| **HIV / AIDS** | retrovirus that destroys CD4 helper T cells; screened by ELISA |
| **Bird flu** | H5N1 avian influenza — from infected poultry |
| **Zika (UPSC 2017)** | Aedes mosquitoes and also sexual transmission; birth defect microcephaly |
| **Japanese encephalitis** | Culex mosquito; pigs and wading birds are hosts; vaccine in endemic districts |
| **Kyasanur Forest Disease ("monkey fever")** | tick-borne virus first found in Karnataka (1957) |
| **Chandipura virus** | spread by sandflies; outbreak among children in Gujarat in 2024 |
| **Human papillomavirus (HPV)** | causes most cervical cancers; prevented by HPV vaccine (Cervavac) |
| **Ebola** | contact with body fluids of infected people or animals (fruit bats) |
| **Mpox PHEIC (clade Ib)** | declared August 2024; ended September 2025 |

### Protozoan and prion diseases

| Disease / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Plasmodium falciparum** | most dangerous malaria parasite — causes cerebral malaria |
| **Plasmodium vivax** | commonest malaria parasite in India |
| **Ronald Ross** | proved mosquitoes transmit malaria, at Secunderabad (1897) — Nobel Prize 1902 |
| **Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis)** | Leishmania donovani, sandfly — endemic in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and UP |
| **Amoebic dysentery** | Entamoeba histolytica — contaminated food and water; houseflies carry it |
| **Sleeping sickness** | Trypanosoma — spread by the tsetse fly (Africa) |
| **Giardiasis** | Giardia — contaminated water; diarrhoea |
| **Prion diseases** | misfolded proteins — mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease |
| **Malaria vaccines** | RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M (WHO-recommended; R21 made by the Serum Institute) |

## Don't confuse
- **Hepatitis A/E = food and water; B/C = blood.** Tattooing can spread **hepatitis B and HIV**, not chikungunya.
- **Salk = injected killed vaccine (IPV); Sabin = oral live vaccine (OPV).**
- **KFD = ticks (Karnataka); Chandipura = sandflies (Gujarat 2024); kala-azar = sandflies (Bihar).**
- **Prions are proteins, not living germs** — no DNA or RNA.

**Remember it:** "Falciparum is fatal, vivax is very common."

**TL;DR**
- Viral: polio (Salk/Sabin), measles (MR), chickenpox (shingles), rabies (Pasteur 1885), hepatitis A/E vs B/C, HIV (CD4, ELISA), H5N1, Zika (sexual too), JE (pigs), KFD (ticks, Karnataka), Chandipura (Gujarat 2024), HPV.
- Protozoan: P. falciparum (deadliest), P. vivax (commonest); Ross at Secunderabad 1897; kala-azar (Bihar); Entamoeba; Trypanosoma.
- Prions: mad cow disease, CJD. Malaria vaccines: RTS,S and R21.
keyPoints: Polio — poliovirus — faecal-oral; Salk (injectable, killed) and Sabin (oral, live) vaccines.
Measles — airborne virus — prevented by the MR (measles-rubella) vaccine.
Plasmodium falciparum — most dangerous malaria parasite — causes cerebral malaria.
Ronald Ross — proved mosquitoes transmit malaria, at Secunderabad (1897) — Nobel Prize 1902.

items.title: Vitamins & Minerals — the Complete Table
items.body:
## Every vitamin and its deficiency

**In one line:** vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and are stored in the body; the B group and C dissolve in water and must be eaten regularly; each has one deficiency disease that examiners pair it with.

**Why it is asked:** "which vitamin is fat-soluble", "Vitamin K is needed for", "folic acid prevents", "pernicious anaemia is caused by lack of", "rickets and osteomalacia" and the UPSC 2014 pair "Vitamin E – night blindness (wrong)" make this one of the most repeated tables.

**The story**

**Vitamin A** keeps the eyes healthy — lack causes night blindness and xerophthalmia. **Vitamin D**, made in the skin from sunlight, builds bones. **Vitamin E** is an antioxidant linked to fertility and healthy skin and cells — **not** night blindness. **Vitamin K** is needed for **blood clotting**; it is injected into newborns. Among the water-soluble vitamins, **B2 (riboflavin)** lack cracks the lips and corners of the mouth (cheilosis), **B9 (folic acid)** prevents **neural-tube defects** in babies, and **B12 (cobalamin)** lack causes **pernicious anaemia**. Minerals matter too: **calcium** for bones (lack → osteoporosis), **iron** for haemoglobin, **iodine** for thyroid hormone, and **zinc** for growth and immunity — while **too much fluoride** causes fluorosis.

### Vitamins and minerals

| Vitamin / mineral | Role and deficiency |
|---|---|
| **Fat-soluble vitamins** | A, D, E and K — stored in the body |
| **Water-soluble vitamins** | B group and C — not stored; needed daily |
| **Vitamin E (tocopherol)** | antioxidant; linked to fertility and healthy cells — not to night blindness |
| **Vitamin K** | needed for blood clotting; given to newborns |
| **Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)** | deficiency cracks the lips and mouth corners (cheilosis) |
| **Vitamin B9 (folic acid)** | prevents neural-tube defects; deficiency causes anaemia |
| **Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)** | deficiency causes pernicious anaemia; found in animal foods |
| **Vitamin D source** | made in the skin from sunlight (UV-B) |
| **Calcium** | bones and teeth; deficiency → osteoporosis |
| **Zinc** | growth and immunity; used with ORS for child diarrhoea |
| **Cretinism** | iodine deficiency in infancy — stunted body and mind |
| **Xerophthalmia** | dry eye from Vitamin A deficiency |

## Don't confuse
- **Night blindness = Vitamin A, not E** (UPSC 2014).
- **Rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults)** are both Vitamin D; **osteoporosis** is mainly calcium loss with age.
- **B9 (folic acid) and B12** both cause anaemia; only **B12** causes **pernicious** anaemia.
- **Vitamin K = clotting**; **Vitamin C = collagen** (scurvy).

**Remember it:** "ADEK in fat; B and C in water."

**TL;DR**
- Fat-soluble A, D, E, K; water-soluble B and C.
- E = antioxidant; K = clotting; B2 = cheilosis; B9 = neural-tube defects; B12 = pernicious anaemia.
- Calcium → osteoporosis; iodine → goitre and cretinism; zinc with ORS.
keyPoints: Fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K — stored in the body.
Water-soluble vitamins — B group and C — not stored; needed daily.

items.title: National Health Programmes, Health Laws & Institutions
items.body:
## The schemes, the Acts and the bodies

**In one line:** India runs disease-control programmes (TB, AIDS, leprosy, vector-borne, mental health, tobacco), mother-and-child schemes (JSY, JSSK, PMSMA, PMMVY, RBSK), and a body of health laws from the Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 to the National Medical Commission Act 2019.

**Why it is asked:** "JSY promotes", "PMSMA is held on the 9th of every month", "Ni-kshay Poshan pays", "the MTP Act now allows abortion up to", "COTPA 2003 bans", "NMC replaced", "ICMR began as" and "World TB Day" are frequent statement and match items.

**The story**

For TB, the **National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP)** — the renamed RNTCP (2020) — pays patients **₹1,000 a month** for nutrition through **Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana** (raised from ₹500 in 2024) and ran a **100-day TB Mukt Bharat campaign** from December 2024. **NACO** runs the National AIDS Control Programme (1992), and the **HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017** bans discrimination against people with HIV. For mothers, **Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005)** pays cash for **institutional delivery**, **JSSK (2011)** makes delivery free, **PMSMA (2016)** gives free antenatal check-ups on the **9th of every month**, and **PMMVY (2017)** gives **₹5,000** for the first child. **RBSK (2013)** screens children for the "**4 Ds**" — defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays. **PM Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana** sells generic medicines cheaply.

The laws: the **Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897** (amended 2020 to protect health workers), the **MTP Act, 1971** (amended 2021: abortion up to **24 weeks** for special categories), the **PCPNDT Act, 1994** (bans sex selection), **COTPA, 2003** (bans smoking in public places and tobacco sale near schools), the **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** (decriminalised attempted suicide) and the **National Medical Commission Act, 2019**, which **replaced the Medical Council of India**.

### National programmes and schemes

| Programme | What it does |
|---|---|
| **NTEP (2020)** | National TB Elimination Programme — the renamed RNTCP |
| **Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana** | ₹1,000 a month nutrition support to TB patients (raised from ₹500 in 2024) |
| **TB Mukt Bharat 100-day campaign** | intensified TB case-finding drive launched December 2024 |
| **National AIDS Control Programme (1992)** | run by NACO; targets 95-95-95 (diagnosed, on treatment, virally suppressed) |
| **NCVBDC** | National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control — malaria, dengue, filariasis, kala-azar, JE, chikungunya |
| **Malaria elimination target** | zero indigenous cases in India by 2030 (National Framework 2016) |
| **Lymphatic filariasis elimination target** | 2027, through mass drug administration |
| **Pulse Polio (1995)** | nationwide oral polio vaccine drives for all children under five |
| **Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005)** | cash incentive for institutional delivery |
| **JSSK (2011)** | Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram — free delivery and newborn care in public hospitals |
| **PMSMA (2016)** | free antenatal check-up on the 9th of every month |
| **PMMVY (2017)** | Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana — ₹5,000 maternity benefit for the first child |
| **RBSK (2013)** | child health screening for the 4 Ds — defects, diseases, deficiencies, developmental delays |
| **RKSK (2014)** | Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram — adolescent health |
| **PM Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana** | cheap generic medicines through Jan Aushadhi Kendras |
| **PM-ABHIM (2021)** | PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission — labs, critical-care blocks, surveillance |
| **Tele-MANAS (2022)** | national tele-mental-health helpline (14416) |
| **75/25 initiative (2023)** | screen and treat 75 million people for hypertension and diabetes by 2025 |

### Health laws

| Law | Key provision |
|---|---|
| **Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897** | oldest epidemic law; amended 2020 to punish violence against health workers |
| **MTP Act, 1971 (amended 2021)** | abortion allowed up to 24 weeks for special categories of women |
| **PCPNDT Act, 1994** | bans sex selection and sex-determination tests |
| **COTPA, 2003** | bans smoking in public places and tobacco sale within 100 yards of schools |
| **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** | right to mental healthcare; decriminalised attempted suicide |
| **HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017** | bans discrimination against people living with HIV |
| **National Medical Commission Act, 2019** | replaced the Medical Council of India |
| **Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994** | regulates organ donation and bans organ trade |
| **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** | created FSSAI (2008), the food regulator |
| **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940** | basis of drug regulation by CDSCO, headed by the DCGI |

### Institutions and health days

| Body / day | Fact |
|---|---|
| **ICMR** | began in 1911 as the Indian Research Fund Association; renamed ICMR in 1949 |
| **National Institute of Virology (NIV)** | Pune — India's top virus lab (isolated SARS-CoV-2 in 2020) |
| **National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC)** | Delhi — disease surveillance (IDSP) |
| **World Health Organization** | founded 7 April 1948, HQ Geneva — 7 April is World Health Day; SEARO is in New Delhi |
| **WHO Pandemic Agreement** | adopted at the World Health Assembly on 20 May 2025 |
| **Gavi** | the Vaccine Alliance (2000), Geneva — funds vaccines for poorer countries |
| **World TB Day** | 24 March — the day Koch announced the TB germ (1882) |
| **World Malaria Day** | 25 April |
| **World AIDS Day** | 1 December |
| **National Doctors' Day** | 1 July — birthday of Dr B.C. Roy |

## Don't confuse
- **JSY = cash for hospital delivery; JSSK = free delivery services; PMMVY = ₹5,000 maternity benefit; PMSMA = check-up on the 9th.**
- **RBSK = children (4 Ds); RKSK = adolescents.**
- **NMC (2019) replaced MCI; FSSAI = food; CDSCO/DCGI = drugs.**
- **World Health Day 7 April; World TB Day 24 March; World Malaria Day 25 April; World AIDS Day 1 December.**

**Remember it:** "PMSMA on the ninth, PMMVY gives five thousand."

**TL;DR**
- NTEP, Ni-kshay Poshan ₹1,000/month, TB Mukt Bharat 100-day campaign; NACO 95-95-95; malaria-free by 2030; filariasis by 2027.
- Mothers and children: JSY 2005, JSSK 2011, PMSMA 2016, PMMVY 2017, RBSK 2013, RKSK 2014.
- Laws: Epidemic Act 1897, MTP 1971/2021 (24 weeks), PCPNDT 1994, COTPA 2003, MHCA 2017, NMC 2019.
- ICMR (1911/1949), NIV Pune, WHO (7 April 1948, Geneva), Pandemic Agreement (May 2025).
keyPoints: NTEP (2020) — National TB Elimination Programme — the renamed RNTCP.
Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana — ₹1,000 a month nutrition support to TB patients (raised from ₹500 in 2024).
Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 — oldest epidemic law; amended 2020 to punish violence against health workers.
MTP Act, 1971 (amended 2021) — abortion allowed up to 24 weeks for special categories of women.
ICMR — began in 1911 as the Indian Research Fund Association; renamed ICMR in 1949.
National Institute of Virology (NIV) — Pune — India's top virus lab (isolated SARS-CoV-2 in 2020).

items.title: Diagnostic Tests, Medical Discoveries & More Andhra Pradesh Health Facts
items.body:
## Tests, pioneers and the AP health map

**In one line:** each disease has a named test (Widal for typhoid, Mantoux for TB, ELISA for HIV, Pap smear for cervical cancer), each vaccine or drug has a pioneer (Jenner, Pasteur, Koch, Fleming, Salk), and Andhra Pradesh has its own health issues and institutions (Uddanam kidney disease, AIIMS Mangalagiri, the Family Doctor programme).

**Why it is asked:** "Mantoux test detects", "Fleming discovered", "Jenner's first vaccine was against", "universal donor blood group", and the AP-specific "Uddanam nephropathy is found in which district" are typical one-markers.

**The story**

**Edward Jenner (1796)** made the first vaccine, against **smallpox**, using cowpox. **Louis Pasteur** made the rabies vaccine (1885); **Robert Koch** found the TB germ (1882); **Alexander Fleming** discovered **penicillin (1928)**, the first antibiotic; **Jonas Salk** made the injectable polio vaccine (1955); and **Banting and Best** isolated **insulin (1921)**. **Karl Landsteiner** discovered the **ABO blood groups (1901)**: **O negative** is the universal donor and **AB positive** the universal recipient.

In Andhra Pradesh, the **Uddanam region of Srikakulam district** has a high burden of **chronic kidney disease of unknown cause (CKDu)**; the state opened a **Kidney Research Centre and Super-Speciality Hospital at Palasa** (2023) for it. **AIIMS Mangalagiri** (Guntur district) is the state's AIIMS. **108 ambulances** began with **EMRI in 2005** in undivided Andhra Pradesh.

### Diagnostic tests

| Test | Detects |
|---|---|
| **Widal test** | typhoid |
| **Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test** | TB infection |
| **TrueNat and CBNAAT** | rapid molecular tests for TB (TrueNat is made in India) |
| **ELISA / Western blot** | HIV (ELISA screens; Western blot confirms) |
| **Pap smear** | early cervical cancer |
| **Schick test** | diphtheria immunity |
| **NS1 antigen test** | early dengue |
| **RT-PCR** | RNA viruses such as SARS-CoV-2 (gold standard for COVID-19) |
| **HbA1c** | average blood sugar over about three months (diabetes) |

### Medical pioneers

| Pioneer | Discovery |
|---|---|
| **Edward Jenner (1796)** | first vaccine — against smallpox, using cowpox |
| **Alexander Fleming (1928)** | penicillin — the first antibiotic |
| **Karl Landsteiner (1901)** | ABO blood groups; O negative = universal donor, AB positive = universal recipient |
| **Banting and Best (1921)** | isolated insulin |
| **Jonas Salk (1955)** | injectable (killed) polio vaccine |
| **Joseph Lister** | antiseptic surgery (carbolic acid) |
| **Christiaan Barnard (1967)** | first human heart transplant |
| **Louise Brown (1978)** | world's first IVF (test-tube) baby; India's first — Durga (Kanupriya Agarwal), 1978 |

### Andhra Pradesh health facts

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Uddanam nephropathy** | chronic kidney disease of unknown cause in the Uddanam region, Srikakulam district |
| **Palasa kidney centre** | government Kidney Research Centre and Super-Speciality Hospital at Palasa (Srikakulam), opened 2023 |
| **AIIMS Mangalagiri** | Andhra Pradesh's AIIMS, in Guntur district |
| **EMRI (2005)** | started the 108 ambulance service in undivided Andhra Pradesh |
| **Fluorosis districts** | Prakasam and Rayalaseema districts (high-fluoride groundwater) |
| **Dr NTR Vaidya Seva budget (2026-27)** | about ₹4,000 crore to the Dr NTR Vaidya Seva Trust |

## Don't confuse
- **Widal = typhoid; Mantoux = TB; ELISA = HIV screening; Western blot = HIV confirmation; Pap smear = cervical cancer.**
- **Jenner = first vaccine (smallpox); Pasteur = rabies vaccine; Fleming = penicillin.**
- **O negative gives to all; AB positive receives from all.**
- **Uddanam (Srikakulam) = kidney disease; Prakasam and Rayalaseema = fluorosis.**

**Remember it:** "Jenner '96, Landsteiner 1901, Fleming '28, Salk '55."

**TL;DR**
- Tests: Widal, Mantoux, TrueNat/CBNAAT, ELISA/Western blot, Pap smear, NS1, RT-PCR, HbA1c.
- Pioneers: Jenner, Fleming, Landsteiner, Banting & Best, Salk, Lister, Barnard, Louise Brown.
- AP: Uddanam CKDu (Srikakulam), Palasa kidney centre, AIIMS Mangalagiri, EMRI 108 (2005).
keyPoints: Widal test — typhoid.
Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test — TB infection.
Edward Jenner (1796) — first vaccine — against smallpox, using cowpox.
Alexander Fleming (1928) — penicillin — the first antibiotic.
Uddanam nephropathy — chronic kidney disease of unknown cause in the Uddanam region, Srikakulam district.
Palasa kidney centre — government Kidney Research Centre and Super-Speciality Hospital at Palasa (Srikakulam), opened 2023.

items.title: For Mains — Health, Diseases & Public Health
items.body:
### For Mains — Health, diseases and public health

**In one line**
For Paper-5, treat health as a development and governance challenge: argue how India moves toward Universal Health Coverage while fighting a double disease burden.

**Why it is asked**
The syllabus clause covers "Human diseases & microbial infections; vaccines; immuno-diagnosis", and Paper-5 development themes, so answers must link schemes, evidence and the way forward.

**The story**
Mains questions here ask you to **evaluate**, not list — the UHC architecture, the double burden of malnutrition and NCDs, or India's eradication record. Build answers around dimensions and quote dated milestones and schemes.

**Picture it**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Burden | Communicable (TB, dengue, Nipah), NCDs (now most deaths), malnutrition |
| Financing | Out-of-pocket spend high; NHP 2017 target 2.5% of GDP |
| Schemes | Ayushman Bharat/PM-JAY (₹5 lakh), Vay Vandana (70+), ABDM, NHM, POSHAN |
| Human resources | ASHA workers, doctor shortage and rural-urban maldistribution |
| Successes | Smallpox 1980, polio-free 2014, trachoma 2024, UIP, Mission Indradhanush |
| Way forward | Higher public spend, primary-care focus, One Health, AMR containment |

**Facts to quote**
- **PM-JAY** ₹5 lakh cover; **Ayushman Vay Vandana (2024)** for all aged 70+.
- Milestones: polio-free **2014**, maternal-neonatal tetanus **2015**, trachoma **2024**; TB elimination targeted **2025**.
- Current threats: **Mpox PHEIC (Aug 2024)**, **HMPV (2025)**, **AMR (NAP-AMR 2017)**.
- AP angle: **Dr NTR Vaidya Seva (Aarogyasri)**, the **108 (EMRI)** ambulance model pioneered in AP, strong AP indicators (TFR below replacement, IMR/MMR better than national).

**Terms explained**
- **Universal Health Coverage (UHC)** = all people get quality care without financial hardship.
- **Immuno-diagnosis** = detecting disease via antibody-antigen reactions (ELISA, rapid kits).

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite PM-JAY plus NHM to show India's two-track UHC push.
- Quote: the NHP 2017 "2.5% of GDP" target to critique under-financing.
- Diagram idea: a two-pan balance — undernutrition on one side, NCDs on the other (the double burden).

**TL;DR**
- Frame health as UHC + the double burden, not a disease list.
- Anchor with Ayushman Bharat, NHM, UIP and the NHP 2017 financing target.
- Quote dated eradication/elimination milestones and current threats (Mpox, AMR).
- Bring the AP angle: Aarogyasri, the 108 EMRI model, and strong AP indicators.
